zh: B 是 A 的前缀最小值序列，单调不增；它的不同值个数等于 A 中“严格前缀最小值”位置（记录点）的个数：第一个位置总是记录点，之后的位置只有严格小于左边所有数时才是。
一次只把某个 A[p] 减小。p 左边的记录点不变；p 是否成为记录点只看新值是否小于它前面最近的记录点的值；若 p 是（或成为）记录点，右边紧接着的那些值不小于新 A[p] 的记录点都要被删掉，遇到第一个更小的就停。每个位置被插入的次数有限，所以删除总次数是摊还线性的。
用 64 位整数保存真实 A，用树状数组保存每个位置是否为记录点的 0/1 标记，前缀和给出排名，按排名二分（倍增）找第 k 个记录点；每次查询先 A[p]−=x，求 p 的排名，若 p 不是记录点就与前驱记录点比较，不更小则答案不变，否则插入 p；随后反复取 p 之后的下一个记录点，只要它的值不小于 A[p] 就删除；输出当前记录点个数。
en: B is the prefix-minimum sequence of A and is non-increasing; its number of distinct values equals the number of strict prefix-minimum positions (records) of A: the first position is always a record, and a later position is one only when it is strictly smaller than everything to its left.

Each query only lowers one value A[p]. Records left of p do not change; whether p becomes a record depends only on whether its new value is smaller than the nearest record before it; if p is (or becomes) a record, the records right after it whose values are not less than the new A[p] must be removed, stopping at the first smaller one. Each position is inserted a bounded number of times, so the total number of removals is linear in the amortized sense.

Keep the real A in 64-bit integers and a Fenwick tree of 0/1 flags marking record positions; prefix sums give ranks, and binary lifting finds the k-th record; for each query do A[p] -= x, compute p's rank, and if p is not a record compare it with the preceding record: if it is not smaller the answer is unchanged, otherwise insert p; then repeatedly take the next record after p and remove it while its value is not less than A[p]; output the current number of records.

explanationEn:
## Pinned source and example correction

fastprep/infosys/infosys-number-of-unique-elements-after-modifications.md in the pinned commit e66f809f4c953bce129f68491726176615db6afc gives in full n,m≤100000, initial 1≤A[i]≤10^9, and the query fields 1≤Q[i][j]≤100000. So the decrement x is explicitly positive, not "no non-negativity guarantee given" as the old blocked note claimed. A query position must also satisfy 1≤L≤n, which is the requirement that the original operation A[L−1] refers to a valid index; this site discloses this implicit condition explicitly and does not turn out-of-range access into an extra business rule.

Each query only permanently subtracts x from A[L−1], then computes an independent B from the modified A: B[0]=A[0], B[i]=min(B[i−1],A[i]). B must not be written back into A. The original text does not restrict modified values to be non-negative, and this site keeps negative results; the minimum can reach 1−100000×100000=−9999999999, so 64-bit integers should be used.

The original input [5,7,2,2,4] with queries [(3,5),(5,4)] is kept, but the original output [2,3] and its explanation did not apply the first query: by the rules, after the first step A=[5,7,−3,2,4] and B=[5,5,−3,−3,−3]; after the second step A=[5,7,−3,2,0] and B is still [5,5,−3,−3,−3]. The correct output is [2,2]. The package explicitly corrects this rather than claiming to reproduce the original wrong answer. The other two public examples are this site's additions. No upstream code was executed.

## Approach

B is non-increasing, and its number of distinct values equals the number of strict prefix-minimum positions (records) of A: the first position is always a record, and a later position is a record only if it is strictly smaller than every element to its left. The record values, in position order, are strictly decreasing.

Lowering A[p] does not change the records to the left of p. If p was not a record and its new value is still not less than the value of its preceding record, the record set does not change; otherwise insert p (if it was already a record, only its value is updated). Starting from the record after p, delete every record whose value is greater than or equal to the new A[p], stopping at the first smaller value; the remaining later records need no change.

Use a Fenwick tree storing a 0/1 flag for whether each position is a record; prefix sums give a record's rank, and binary lifting by rank finds the preceding and following record positions, supporting insertion and deletion. The real A is stored separately, and non-record positions also keep their own original values; they must not be replaced by their prefix minimum.

## Proof of correctness

Records correspond one-to-one to the distinct values of B: each time a strictly smaller A value is met, the prefix minimum gains exactly one new smaller value; otherwise it keeps its previous value. So it suffices to maintain the record set exactly.

One decrease only affects position p and the positions to its right. Everything before p is unchanged; whether p becomes a record is decided entirely by comparing the new A[p] with its preceding record (that is, the previous prefix minimum). If it does not become a record, all prefix minima stay unchanged. If it becomes or remains a record, the following old records whose values are greater than or equal to A[p] no longer strictly improve the minimum and must therefore be deleted; the first smaller old record and the records after it have strictly decreasing values and all remain records.

Other positions that were not records and were not modified cannot become records because some value to their left decreased. Therefore no additional insertion position is missed. Initialization scans directly to obtain the exact records, and the update steps above are complete, necessary and sufficient; induction over the queries shows that every output is correct.

## Amortized complexity and values

Each query inserts at most the modified position, once. Initially there are at most n records and there are at most m insertions in total, so even if a position is deleted and later reinserted, the total number of deletions does not exceed n+m. Each predecessor query, insertion, deletion and successor search costs O(log n), and each query performs at most one successor check that does not trigger a deletion. Total time O((n+m) log n), space O(n+m) (including input and output). The inner deletion loop must not be mistaken for a scan of the whole array on every query. Actual array values may drop to about −10^10, so use 64 bits; the Fenwick tree only stores counts of at most n.

## Independent verification and full boundaries

The oracle copies A directly, modifies only the specified element for each query, then rebuilds the prefix minima B with a full scan and counts the distinct values with a set; it uses no record set, Fenwick tree or amortized property. 163 unique inputs were compared through real subprocesses.

The full n=m=100000 cases include deleting records one by one in a strictly decreasing array, the tail decreasing repeatedly while all records are kept, the head deleting all records at once, the same position lowered repeatedly to near −10^10, alternating head and tail updates that cause repeated insertions and deletions, and positions in reverse order deleting old records with equal new values. For the large boundary cases all one hundred thousand expected outputs are determined from direct structural patterns, not generated by the reference program. Two negative controls respectively keep equal successors and subtract from the previous B instead of the real A; they count as successfully rejected only after exiting normally.
